stories.topic: Offending a committee with the word 'zombie'
stories.summary: Years ago Ajay sat on the Percy Mistry committee on making Bombay an international financial centre. He and Percy kept using the term 'zombie bank' freely, and some committee members were offended because they thought it was a disrespectful word. Ajay's point is that 'zombie firm' and 'zombie bank' are technical terms that came out of the research on Japan.
stories.insight: Being uncomfortable with blunt words for failure is itself part of the sentimentality Ajay argues against. You cannot deal with dead-men-walking institutions if you will not call them that.
stories.quote: And there Percy and I were merrily bandying the word zombie bank around. And some people in the committee got very offended.

stories.topic: The bankruptcy code that was promised but never written
stories.summary: Montek Singh Ahluwalia, then deputy chairman of the Planning Commission, told the Ministry of Company Affairs that the new Companies Act of 2013 should contain a full bankruptcy code, with collective negotiation among creditors. He was assured it would be done. It wasn't. When Ajay later raised the issue, Montek asked whether he was sure it wasn't in the Act. Ajay had read the statute: it had only trivial winding-up provisions and no bankruptcy process.
stories.insight: A promise made in a ministry is not law on paper. A real bankruptcy code is a negotiation mechanism for creditors, which is very different from winding-up clauses. It took a long time, and someone who actually read the law, for that basic point to land.
stories.quote: I said, I have done my fair share of bedtime reading of the Companies Act. And there is some trivial winding up provisions, but there is no bankruptcy process in the Companies Act.

stories.topic: How one budget paragraph grew into the IBC
stories.summary: Ajay retells a story KP Krishnan told on The Seen and the Unseen. The 2015 budget speech carried a paragraph from the small and medium enterprises ministry promising a bankruptcy code for small companies. Krishnan went to Jaitley and asked whether they could aim higher, with a full bankruptcy code. Jaitley asked whether they had the ability and the teams. Krishnan pointed to the FSLRC, which had shown India could run large research teams and draft complex laws to a world-class standard. That led to the BLRC, chaired by TK Viswanathan, with Ajay and Susan Thomas as members. The committee started with a narrow plan to amend winding-up provisions. Rajiv Mehrishi, then secretary of the Department of Economic Affairs, backed the more radical goal of a full code. Susan led the team that wrote the first draft, which became the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code in 2016.
stories.insight: Big reform needs an ambitious ask and a believable answer to 'can we actually do this?'. Here that answer came from capability the FSLRC had built earlier. Even so, the narrow vision had to be overcome before the real project began.
stories.quote: And Jaitley was like, Do we have the ability? Do we have the teams?

stories.summary: After 1986, Japan's Ministry of Finance and MITI ran an industrial policy that kept bad firms alive through bad banks. These zombie firms kept competing with healthy ones and destroyed their profitability across the economy. Ajay says this cost Japan thirty years of economic dynamism.
stories.insight: Keeping dead firms alive is not kindness. It drains the profits that healthy firms need in order to invest, and the bill can run for decades.
stories.quote: Japan went through thirty years of misery because they had zombie banks which were keeping zombie firms aloft.

stories.summary: The original draft of the bankruptcy law set out how to build the new regulator, the IBBI, in about 140 sections covering checks and balances, separation of powers and governance, at FSLRC-level quality. All of it was deleted. Someone instead copied about eight sections from the SEBI Act, which brought SEBI's malfunctions into the IBBI. The regulator then hit state-capability limits from day one, along with the usual pull toward grabbing more power for itself.
stories.insight: Institutional quality is decided in dull drafting details. One shortcut can lock a new regulator into an old regulator's flaws.
stories.quote: And some people just chose to cut and paste some eight sections from the SEBI Act into the IBBI. So all the bad practices of how SEBI malfunctions were brought into IBBI.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay explains how he and Vijay Kelkar 'zero base' public policy to find the essentials of civilisation; the show notes link their book.
recommendations.reason: The co-authors' framework for deciding which parts of the state must be fixed first, given very scarce reform capacity.

core_ideas.concept: Creative destruction needs Shiva as well as Vishnu
core_ideas.explanation: Schumpeter's account of progress: innovators take risks and earn a temporary monopoly rent on a new idea, and the prospect of that rent drives research and business-model innovation. Old firms that cannot keep up go bankrupt. Their labour and capital are not lost; they flow back to other firms, the way the atoms in our bodies return to other forms of life. Ajay maps this onto the Hindu ideas of creation, preservation and destruction: interfere with any one of them and the balance breaks.
core_ideas.quote: So to take interest in firms is to take interest in birth and death. Schumpeterian creative destruction requires both. You need the creation of firms, you need Vishnu, and you need Shiv.

core_ideas.concept: A complex, changing world: adapt or make way
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's two axioms are that the world is complex and that it is constantly changing, so needs cannot be met by central planning. Firms that meet needs earn profits. Those that stop adapting, meaning they stop learning how to keep serving others, should go out of business so their resources can be used elsewhere. Ajay adds that a firm's way of organising labour and capital is like an organism's DNA: we get attached to it, but the recipe can be bad or the world can move on. Some firms do transform; Tata Steel of 2024 is unrecognisable from Jamsetji Tata's. Many won't.
core_ideas.quote: One of them is that the world is complex, and the other one is that the world is in flux.

core_ideas.concept: Default hands the firm to the creditors
core_ideas.explanation: As the company was conceived in 15th–16th century Europe, shareholders run the firm only while they service their debts, and creditors have no say. On default, the only questions before a judge should be whether there was credit and whether there was a default. Shareholders are then thrown out and usually wiped out, and the firm is rebuilt on a new balance sheet controlled by the creditors. Suppliers owed money are creditors just as much as lenders, and should not be treated as second-class.
core_ideas.quote: So it's a very dramatic fact about the concept of a limited liability company, that shareholders are in charge of the company as long as they are meeting their dues. The day the shareholders fail to pay their dues, they're supposed to get thrown out and replaced by the creditors.

core_ideas.explanation: Indian thinking tends to get emotional about a company and its founding family. Ajay insists that equity and debt are cold relationships. Business failure is normal: people and firms should take risks, firms should go bankrupt, and bankruptcy should carry no stigma. What matters is a well-defined script for what happens after a default.
core_ideas.quote: The word stakeholder is a sure sign of feeble reasoning. What is needed here is cold business reasoning.

core_ideas.explanation: A failing firm propped up with more debt, because badly regulated banks won't admit the problem or the government leans on them, keeps competing with healthy firms and eats their margins. Without profits, healthy firms don't invest, and dynamism drains from the whole economy. Ajay's example: a kept-alive Air India or Jet Airways sells cheap tickets and harms quality airlines like Vistara.
core_ideas.quote: These firms that are dead men walking are called zombie firms. By the way, by symmetry, the banks that are dead men walking are called zombie banks.

core_ideas.concept: The melting ice cube: speed is everything
core_ideas.explanation: Once a firm is in trouble, insiders know first. Key employees leave, suppliers hold back goods, and maintenance is skipped. A promoter family that knows more than outsiders may start quietly taking cash out. Every delay destroys value and gives the family more time to extract cash. A healthy system needs an objective early warning that triggers the bankruptcy process quickly.
core_ideas.quote: Once a firm starts getting into trouble, it's a melting ice cube. It rapidly falls apart.

core_ideas.concept: Going concern vs liquidation is a business call
core_ideas.explanation: A firm is more than its factory and offices. Its people, processes, IT systems, culture and outside relationships add up to intangible capital that is often worth a lot. Caught early, the firm may fetch more sold as a running business than broken up. Caught late, only liquidation is left. Creditors must compare the two (say 40 from liquidation against 70 from a sale as a going concern) as a commercial judgment, not a humanitarian one.
core_ideas.quote: If you get there soon enough, actually the value of the firm as a going concern is higher than the sum of the parts.

core_ideas.concept: The committee of creditors as a bargaining table
core_ideas.explanation: Creditors' interests clash. A secured creditor holding a key factory can threaten to wreck a going-concern plan unless paid first. Decisions need a supermajority, not just 51%. Many good bids are not all-cash; they are promises to repay over years, which forces a judgment about whether to trust the bidder. India's instinct is to turn this into rule-bound, procurement-style bid opening, because its financial firms are bureaucracies. That is a central bottleneck.
core_ideas.quote: What we want is a badass commercially sophisticated committee of creditors that is able to view these risks and make deals and do negotiations and come up with a value maximizing answer.

core_ideas.concept: The loss has already happened, and banks want to hide it
core_ideas.explanation: By the time of bankruptcy the loss is real; the only question is who bears it. Indian banks, especially public-sector ones, keep the loan on their books at full value and delay recognising the loss, including through evergreening (lending the borrower fresh money to repay the old loan). They also fear future CBI investigations, so they act to look good later rather than to recover the most money. Ajay's unorthodox second-best fix: until banking regulation improves, cut banks' voting power in the committee of creditors, since mutual funds, foreign institutional investors, NBFCs and insurers are more commercial.
core_ideas.quote: So a core insight in bankruptcy is a business has failed, the loss has already taken place. Now all we are debating is who is going to bear the loss.

core_ideas.concept: Promoters, poison pills and secret deals
core_ideas.explanation: India bars promoters from bidding for their own bankrupt firm. Ajay thinks this is a mistake in principle: promoters know the business best and would likely bid higher. But he accepts the counter-argument. A promoter who expects to return could plant hidden traps that only they can defuse, scaring off other bidders, and weak rule of law means this goes unpunished. The result is two bad extremes: promoters are shut out of formal bankruptcy, while banks quietly restructure loans with them in secret.
core_ideas.quote: Poison pill is where the promoter leaves messy things inside the company that she knows about, that she understands, that she will be able to defuse once she is back in charge, but the new person will stumble on a landmine because they don't know what is going on.

core_ideas.concept: Market practice vs waiting for the regulator
core_ideas.explanation: In the UK, bankruptcy practice grew for centuries out of common law and the way business was actually done, and was written into law only late. India expects every step to be written down in law and regulation, so banks won't act without a rule, and outcomes depend on the regulator's quality and its one-size-fits-all rules. Ajay sees this as losing sight of how a market economy works, where creditors negotiate and write contracts that suit them.
core_ideas.quote: We are so coded into expecting everything to be written in laws and regulations.

core_ideas.concept: Judge a reform by outcomes: life in the shadow of the law
core_ideas.explanation: Inputs are the law, the NCLT and the committees. Outputs are the bankruptcy cases and how much creditors recover. The outcome that matters is a better credit market: borrowers keen to repay, lenders willing to lend, and more borrowing overall. In advanced economies, most disputes never reach court because everyone negotiates privately, knowing what the law would do.
core_ideas.quote: In advanced economies, most transactions are privately negotiated between the creditors and the shareholders under the threat of the law. So the term used is in the shadow of the law.

core_ideas.concept: No good law in a vacuum
core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues that 'the law' is more than the written statute. It includes the invisible infrastructure of state capability and people's reasonable expectations that the law will be enforced, and when that is broken, the whole commercial culture suffers. Ajay frames the choice as a trade-off. Pass a strong law that underperforms today and improves as the environment catches up, or settle for a weaker compromise suited to current conditions.
core_ideas.quote: there is nothing called a good law or a good policy in a vacuum.

core_ideas.explanation: Policy improves through a pipeline: data sets, researchers, working papers, blogs, competing proposals and op-eds criticising the status quo. Ministers and secretaries cannot generate this knowledge themselves. Policy-support organisations that place fluent young staff with officials are a staffing arrangement, not intellectual leadership. India briefly had a bankruptcy research community, but it scattered. Ajay estimates about two papers a year appear where twenty are needed, and without criticism nothing gets fixed.
core_ideas.quote: And I think most people in India don't understand the importance of the knowledge ecosystem. That every area of work has to be ensconced in a successful knowledge ecosystem.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay attributes the 1991–2011 successes to many reforms moving at once (capital controls, the equity market, software, telecom), each strengthening the others. Bankruptcy reform suffered because the parallel fix to banking regulation never happened, so badly regulated banks became weak players inside the new process.
core_ideas.quote: So when many, many policy projects are moving, it's actually a virtuous cycle, it strengthens everything.

core_ideas.explanation: Reform capacity, research talent and philanthropic money are very scarce, so priorities matter. Ajay and Vijay Kelkar start by listing what civilisation and a market economy cannot do without: foreign policy, the military, fiat money, criminal justice, police and courts, a tax system to pay for them, and commercial law and financial regulation. These come first, ahead of causes that feel more urgent on humanitarian grounds, such as health.
core_ideas.quote: give me a list of the elements of the state of public policy that are essential for civilization, that without that, you will be in barbarism.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening: 'Firms are awesome, firms are amazing, firms are edifying, firms are illuminating, and when firms are sexually aroused, firms are firm.'
When Ajay casts creative destruction as Vishnu and Shiva, Amit asks: 'Am I sitting with Ajay Shah or am I sitting with my friend Devdutt Pattanaik?'
Amit told a creator friend who wanted to start a vlog to 'throw things at the wall'. 'Five minutes later he calls back and says the camera broke. So this is not always great advice.'

Amit on Japan: it 'not only had zombie firms and zombie banks, she also made a lot of great zombie movies'. He wonders whether to rewatch them for deeper metaphor beyond the surface: 'dead man walking, axe in hand, hand chopped off.'
Ajay, on checking whether the Companies Act 2013 had a bankruptcy code: 'I have done my fair share of bedtime reading of the Companies Act.'
Ajay on whether lenders keep getting fooled by misbehaving promoters: 'The credit markets in India are medium foolish. They are not deeply foolish.'
Amit worries that bankers on a committee won't know the first thing about biscuits. Ajay: 'They gave you hundred crore rupees... At that time, they're bloody well going to understand your industry.'
Amit introduces the committee of creditors as 'a CoC, a cock as it were.'
On poison pills, Amit pictures 'a rat trap in the corner office under the chair under the table.' Ajay: 'That's literally what can be done.'
After Ajay grades his own creation a 'C grade' bankruptcy process, Amit protests that the work of Ajay, Susan and Bhargavi is 'being dismissed by some random uncle as third rate.'
Ajay describes the insolvency professional who oversees the whole process as 'a bit of a maître d''.

Hindu trinity: Ajay maps creation, preservation and destruction onto the life cycle of firms, with bankruptcy as Shiva's work. 'If you'd interfere with any one of them, the great balance of the universe would be disrupted.'
Joseph Schumpeter: innovators earn a temporary monopoly rent on new ideas, which funds research, while firms that can't keep up die and free their labour and capital.
Tata Steel: Ajay's proof that old dogs can learn new tricks. 'Tata Steel of 2024 is unrecognizably different from the original Tata Steel of Jamsetji Tata.'
North and Williamson: invoked for the institutional-economics idea that institutions create the conditions for people to enter complex contracts.

SARFAESI Act, 2002: India's first milestone, giving secured creditors rights over collateral. In Ajay's example, if Amit pledges 'that pretty microphone' and defaults, the lender can seize it. With no forum for creditors to negotiate collectively, it pushed everything toward liquidation.

FSLRC (Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission), led by Justice Srikrishna from 2011 to 2015: it built a specialised bankruptcy framework for banks and insurers and became the model for the BLRC.
'Sunlight is the best disinfectant': the quip that follows Ajay's point that banks prefer to negotiate in darkness, one creditor at a time.
'Turtles all the way down': Amit's phrase for how a law broken at its foundations, in enforcement and state capability, damages the whole commercial culture built on top of it.
The hosts riff that 'internationalization' should really be said 'I eighteen N'.
